lessons.title: uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco — counting to five

segments.text: Numbers are the most reused words in any language — and Spanish counts almost exactly like Latin, which means you already half-know them from English. Here are 1 to 5, each with the English words it planted.
diphthong-ue — cuatro = KWA-tro (the cu- is a kw glide).
r-tap — soft taps in tres, cuatro.

utterances: Spanish: uno (1). from Latin: ūnus. English cousins: unit, union, unique, unanimous, universe (and a/an, one).
Spanish: dos (2). from Latin: duo. English cousins: duo, dual, duet, double, duplex.
Spanish: tres (3). from Latin: trēs. English cousins: trio, triple, trinity, trident, triangle.
Spanish: cuatro (4). from Latin: quattuor. English cousins: quart, quarter, quadrant, square (Latin qu- becomes Spanish cu-).
Spanish: cinco (5). from Latin: quīnque. English cousins: quintet, quintessence, quintuplet (Latin qu- becomes Spanish c-).

segments.text: So cinco and quintet are the same number — Latin quīnque just softened its qu- to a Spanish c-. Count the family on your fingers: unit, duo, trio, quart, quint.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: uno becomes un / una

segments.text: uno shrinks before a noun: un (masc.) / una (fem.) — and these double as "a/an" (Spanish makes no difference between "one" and "a"): un café = "a coffee / one coffee." The others (dos, tres…) don't change.

segments.instruction: "uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco" — count up
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco" — count up]

segments.instruction: "un café, una cerveza" — uno becomes un/una before a noun
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "un café, una cerveza" — *uno* → un/una before a noun]

segments.text: Give 1–5 in Spanish. (Uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco.) What English word is cinco the cousin of, and why does it look different? (Quintet — Latin quīnque's qu- became Spanish c-.) What two things does un/una mean? ("One" and "a/an.") Next: 6–10.

lessons.title: seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez — and the calendar's secret
lessons.gloss: the numbers 6–10 (and the months hidden in them)

segments.text: The rest of the way to ten — and these four hide a fact that explains the English calendar: September through December are just Latin for 7, 8, 9, 10.
diphthong-ie — siete = SYE-teh, nueve = NWE-veh (the ie/ue glide, a Spanish signature).

utterances: Spanish: seis (6). from Latin: sex. English cousins: sextet, sextant, semester (six months).
Spanish: siete (7). from Latin: septem. English cousins: September (the 7th month!), septet, septuagenarian.
Spanish: ocho (8). from Latin: octō. English cousins: October (8th), octopus, octave, octagon.
Spanish: nueve (9). from Latin: novem. English cousins: November (9th), novena.
Spanish: diez (10). from Latin: decem. English cousins: December (10th), decimal, decade, dime, decimate.

segments.text: Why are the "7th–10th" months numbered 7–10 when they sit at 9–12? Because the old Roman year began in March — so September really was the 7th month. Julius and Augustus later inserted July and August (named for themselves), shoving the counting-months out of place, but the Latin numbers stuck. Every time you say December, you're saying Roman "ten."

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: building the teens (a fusion)

segments.text: Past ten, Spanish fuses "ten and X" into one word:
diez y seis ("ten and six") becomes dieciséis (16).
diez y siete becomes diecisiete (17), and so on to 19.
English did the identical thing: six + ten becomes sixteen. So dieciséis and sixteen are built the same way, from the same two numbers.

segments.text: Give 6–10. (Seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez.) Why is December Latin for "ten"? (The Roman year started in March, so the 10th month was December.) How do you make 16, and what English word matches? (diez y seis becomes dieciséis; sixteen.) Next: the verb for having — tener.

lessons.title: tener — "to have," your first irregular verb
lessons.gloss: to have (your first irregular / stem-changing verb)

segments.text: Every verb so far has been regular — hablo, como, vivo, all tidy. tener ("to have") is your first irregular one, and it breaks the rule in the two ways Spanish verbs most often do. Meet the exceptions now; you'll see them again and again.
diphthong-ie — the stem grows a -ie-: tienes = TYE-nes.
tener comes from Latin tenēre, "to hold, to keep, to grasp." Having is, at root, holding. That root has a firm grip on English:
tenant (one who holds land), tenure, tenacious (holding on), tenable, tenet (a held belief).
with prefixes: contain ("hold together"), retain ("hold back"), maintain ("hold in hand"), sustain ("hold up"), detain, obtain.
tener misbehaves in exactly the two classic Spanish ways:
The yo form is odd: not "teno" but tengo (a -g- appears). Several common verbs do this (hago, pongo, salgo, vengo).
The stem vowel breaks e becomes ie in the stressed forms — a stem-changer:

Notice tenemos keeps the plain e — the vowel only cracks to ie when it's stressed. That "boot" pattern (all forms but nosotros/vosotros) is the single most common irregularity in Spanish; tener is your model for it.

segments.instruction: "tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tienen" — hear the ie crack in, and drop out for tenemos
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tienen" — hear the *ie* crack in, and drop out for *tenemos*]

segments.instruction: "tener" then English "tenant, retain, contain" — the hold family
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "tener" then English "tenant, retain, contain" — the *hold* family]

segments.text: What Latin verb is tener from, and its English cousins? (tenēre, "to hold" — tenant, retain, contain.) Its two irregularities? (The -go yo-form tengo; the e becomes ie stem-change tienes/tiene/tienen.) Which form keeps the plain e? (tenemos — it's unstressed.) Next: use it to give your age.

lessons.title: ¿Cuántos años tienes? — "how old are you?"
lessons.gloss: how old are you? (literally "how many years do you have?")

segments.text: With tener and your numbers, you can ask and give age — and Spanish does it in a way English doesn't: you don't be a number of years old, you have them.
¿Cuántos años tienes? = "How old are you?" literally: "How many years do you have?"

cuántos = "how many," from Latin quantus, "how much/great" becomes English quantity, quantum, quantify. (It's the qu- question family — qué, cómo, dónde, cuántos.) It agrees: cuántos años (masc. pl.).
años = "years," from Latin annus — and look, the ñ is back (the doubled-nn of annus becomes añ, your writing lesson). annus also gives English annual, anniversary, biennial.
tienes = "you have" (the tener you just learned).
Age is had, not been.
This is a real difference to internalize: Spanish counts age with tener ("have"), not ser/estar ("be").
— ¿Cuántos años tienes? — Tengo veinte años. ("I have twenty years.")
Saying "soy veinte" ("I am twenty") is simply wrong in Spanish. You possess your years; you don't equal them. (French and Italian do the same — j'ai vingt ans, ho vent'anni, all "I have.")

segments.instruction: answer — "Tengo ___ años" with your own number
segments.source: [YOU SAY: answer — "Tengo ___ años" with your own number]

segments.instruction: never "soy ___"; always "tengo ___ años" — age is had
segments.source: [YOU SAY: never "soy ___"; always "tengo ___ años" — age is *had*]

segments.text: What does ¿Cuántos años tienes? literally ask? ("How many years do you have?") Which verb gives age in Spanish — ser or tener? (tener — you have your years.) What letter does años bring back, and from what? (The ñ, from Latin annus's doubled nn.) Next: put counting and age together in practice.

lessons.title: Practice — numbers, having, and age
lessons.gloss: counting, having, and telling your age

segments.text: Two new powers this chapter: you can count and you can talk about what you have (including your years). Drill the numbers and the irregular tener until both are automatic.
Count up: uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco, seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez.
tener, all forms: tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tienen (mind the tengo and the e becomes ie crack).
— Hola. ¿Cómo te llamas? — Me llamo Ana. ¿Y cuántos años tienes? — Tengo veintiuno. ¿Y tú? — Tengo diecinueve. — Un café, por favor. ¿Cuánto es? — Dos euros.
numbers 1–10 ( from ūnus … decem; cinco/quintet, diez/December), and the teen fusion diez y seis becomes dieciséis (= sixteen).
tener — "to have" ( from tenēre "hold"; tenant/retain/contain), your first irregular / stem-changing verb: tengo, and e becomes ie (tienes).
¿Cuántos años tienes? — age with tener ("have your years," not "be"); años from annus (the ñ).

segments.source: [YOU SAY: count 1–10 up and back down]

Count to five. (Uno … cinco.) Give the yo and tú of tener, and name its two irregularities. (Tengo / tienes; the -go yo-form and the e becomes ie stem-change.) How does Spanish give age? (With tener — "I have X years.") Next chapter: ser vs estar head-on — the two "to be" verbs, sorted for good.
